site.name: Tōkaidō Review
site.concept: A long-form editorial journal tracing the artisans, post-towns, and printed images of late Edo-period Japan.

card_pattern: Cards are plain off-white panels framed only by a 1px sumi hairline on the left edge. Each card carries a single small kamon (umebachi or matsu) in its upper-right corner at ~24px, the article kicker set in indigo small-caps, the title in Shippori Mincho display weight, and a thin sumi divider before a 3-line dek in Inter. No drop shadows, no rounded corners — generous internal padding (32–48px) so the negative space frames the type.
design_rules: Asymmetric off-center compositions with at least 30% of every screen left deliberately blank — ma is structural. Sumi-on-kraft is the default, indigo carries emphasis, cinnabar is reserved for the seal accent and one hairline rule per page. Wagara only appears as a low-opacity seigaiha background drift; kamon appear as solitary stamps, never repeated.

pages.title: Tōkaidō Review — A Journal of the Edo Period
pages.content_brief: Masthead with vertically-set title 'Tōkaidō Review' offset to the right third, balanced by a single paulownia seal at lower-left. Lead essay teaser: 'The Fifty-Three Stations, Two Hundred Years On' by Mariko Sato, dated Autumn 2024 issue. Beneath: three featured pieces in a staggered column — a Hokusai-print analysis, a profile of a Kyoto indigo dyer, and a field report from Tsumago-juku. Footer kicker: 'Issue XIV — published quarterly from Kanda, Tokyo.'

pages.title: The Fifty-Three Stations, Two Hundred Years On — Tōkaidō Review
pages.content_brief: Long-form essay by Mariko Sato retracing Hiroshige's 1833 Tōkaidō Gojūsan-tsugi series, walking from Nihonbashi to Sanjō Ōhashi over 23 days in May 2024. Narrow single-column body (~62ch), pull-quotes set in Shippori Mincho italic with a vertical sumi rule. Sidebar inset listing the five stations where the original honjin inns still stand. Footnotes reference the Tokyo National Museum print collection and Smith & Poster's 1986 translation.

pages.title: Indigo at Aizome-an — A Studio Visit — Tōkaidō Review
pages.content_brief: Profile of Naoko Furusawa, fifth-generation aizome (indigo) dyer working from a Nishijin machiya in Kyoto. Conversation transcribed in March 2024 covers fermentation of sukumo, the seasonal rhythm of the dye vat, and her decision to refuse synthetic indigo despite a 40% cost gap. Photograph captions describe a 200-year-old kame vat sunk into the earthen floor. Closes with Furusawa's address: 412 Ōmiya-dōri, Kamigyō-ku.

pages.title: Hokusai's Wave, Read Slowly — Tōkaidō Review
pages.content_brief: Close visual reading of 'Kanagawa-oki Nami-ura' (The Great Wave) by critic Junichirō Mori. Argues against the Western reading of the wave as menacing — instead positions it within the seigaiha lineage of repeating, structural water. Includes detail crops of the foam claws, the boats, and Mt. Fuji's diminished scale. Dated 14 September 2024.

pages.title: Field Report — Tsumago-juku in Winter — Tōkaidō Review
pages.content_brief: First-person dispatch from the Nakasendō post-town of Tsumago in Nagano Prefecture, January 2024. Documents the 1968 preservation ordinance, the lacquered shop signs of Terashita-machi, and dinner of gohei-mochi at Matsushiro Inn. Author: Kenji Aoyama, contributing editor. Includes a small map illustration and a closing note on snow accumulation that week (47cm).

pages.title: Masthead & Subscriptions — Tōkaidō Review
pages.content_brief: Editorial masthead listing editor-in-chief Mariko Sato, art director Hisao Tanabe, contributing editors, and the Kanda postal address: 3-7-2 Kanda-Surugadai, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo 101-0062. Subscription terms: ¥2,800 per quarterly issue, ¥10,400 annual. Mission paragraph: a journal devoted to the material culture of the Edo period, published since 2019. Attribution line for kamon and wagara source files (CC-BY-SA, Wikimedia Commons).
